D1 revert: `line_number` is not set on any relationship. It is a PRODUCT field — the indexer stores it (src/ast/parallel-indexer.ts:2789) and the address surfaces serve call-site positions from it (src/intelligence/graph/line-address.ts) — so this is the shape the lane was in for every one of its 1,784 edges: navigable to a symbol, but not to a LINE. Reverted generically by deleting the field from every edge.

D2 revert: the trailing assignment operator is left in the captured name. The grammar's `word` node spans `CGO_ENABLED?` for `?=` but only `CC` for `:=`, so the two spellings disagree. Measured: 55 symbols named `CGO_ENABLED?`/`BUILD_TAGS+`, and 112 edge ends that dangled by construction because every reference names the clean identifier.

D3 revert: references are collected only beneath a `variable_assignment` or a `rule`, so a bare top-level expression contributes nothing. `$(foreach t,… $(eval $(call mk,$(t))))` — the idiom nomad/GNUmakefile uses to reify its package targets — is a `function_call` directly under `makefile`; the corpus has one such site and it produced zero edges.

D4 revert: `$(VAR:.c=.o)` is a `substitution_reference`, a SIBLING of `variable_reference` and not a child of it. Reading only the latter loses every substitution reference — 9 in this corpus, and the one in the fixture is the whole point of that fixture.

D5 revert: `export NAME` with no `=` wraps a `list` and has no assignment node anywhere, so it is the only place that name appears. Ignoring the list form makes the export invisible entirely — 22 `export` lines in this corpus, of which the bare form is a share.

D6 revert: the include edge is sourced at a literal `makefile` instead of this file's module node. With a constant source every makefile that includes `hooks` produces the SAME edge, so two files cannot be told apart in the graph and no include can be attributed to a file.

D7 revert: the BUILTIN / EXTERNAL / PROJECT split is collapsed, every reference becomes `uses`. A variable this file declares then leaves the reference graph, which is how a real declaration gets demoted; and a prerequisite that is only a FILE is published as a project-internal reference, asserting a declaration that does not exist. Measured over the corpus: 231 file-path, 187 external-variable and 160 builtin edge ends are on the wrong side of this line.

D8 revert: only the FIRST `prerequisites` node of a rule is read. The grammar emits one node per `|`-separated group, so an order-only list is a second node — 172 order-only prerequisites in this corpus are invisible if only the first group is taken.

D9 revert: a `$(foreach VAR,…)` binder is labelled `external` instead of `local_binding`. It is neither an external variable nor a project declaration — it is a local introduced by the loop, and pooling it with the 187 genuinely-external names is what makes the `uses` class unreadable.

D10 revert: a computed include (`include $(shell …)`) is dropped. Its target is a `shell_function` node, not the `function_call` an implementer would reach for first, and the target is not knowable at parse time — so the EXPRESSION must be recorded and flagged. A dropped include is invisible; an unresolved one is a fact.

D11 revert: a keyword reaching the name-capture path is accepted as a name. `export` reached it in boundary/Makefile and appeared as the target of six edges — an edge to a keyword is an edge to nothing, and it also means the exported variable was never declared.
D12 revert: a `define` declares a `constant`. A `$(call NAME)` that resolves to a constant is a callee that cannot be called, and the graph's call edges then point at values.

D13 revert: the module node does not `contains` its declarations. GNU Make has exactly one declaration level, so the file node is the only place containment can live — without it, "what does this Makefile declare?" is unanswerable and the module symbol has no outgoing edge at all.

D14 revert: only `export VAR` lines produce exports and a buildable target does not. A target IS the file's public surface — an including makefile invokes it by name — so this is the shape the lane shipped with `exports: []` hardcoded, where the answer to "what does this Makefile offer?" was nothing at all.

D15 revert: a `$(NAME)` prerequisite is recorded under its wrapper text rather than normalised to NAME. The dependency is on the expansion, so the edge target must be the variable — otherwise `all: $(OBJ)` publishes a target named `$(OBJ)` that nothing declares and the reference to OBJ is lost.

D16 revert: `$@`/`$<`/`$^` are labelled `builtin` and `$$?` is too. An automatic variable is a Make builtin read, and `$$?` is the SHELL's exit-status variable because `$$` is Make's escaped dollar — calling it a Make builtin is a category error that hides 212 automatic and 11 shell edge ends inside the builtin bucket.

D18 revert: a rule whose TARGET is an expression publishes no prerequisite edges. `$(BIN): $(OBJS) | builddir` declares no literal target name, so the pre-fix code iterated the empty list of literal targets and dropped the whole rule's dependencies — first group and order-only alike (405 corpus edges). Found by script/m12/make-contract-probe.ts, a gate that had existed for this lane and had never been run; a check that is never executed cannot report the defect it was written for.

Reverts the deferral that keeps `private VAR = v` and `override VAR := v` from losing their flag. The walker reaches the directive BEFORE the assignment nested inside it, so applying the flag at the point of the directive targets a symbol that does not exist yet and the annotation is dropped -- silently, and only in the one-line spelling that is actually written. The two-line form (`VAR = v` then `private VAR = w`) still works, which is why this survived having a code path at all.

REPRODUCES the pre-fix output for `unexport NAME` rather than reverting a line of code: the edge is ADDED BACK, exactly as it survived the unexport before the fix. Mutating an existing relationship cannot express this defect, because after the fix that relationship does not exist -- a transform that looks for it is a silent no-op that would report itself CAUGHT-by-nobody. The shape it adds is the one the pre-fix analyzer published: the symbol table said `isExported: false` while the graph still carried an `exports` edge, so a consumer reading relationships got the opposite answer from one reading symbols.

Reverts the metadata keys from the camelCase the file uses everywhere else (isMakeVariable, isExported, isBuiltin) to the `is${type}` interpolation that produced isprivate / isoverride / isundefine. A key rename is not cosmetic here: those were the names script/m14/spec/make-completeness.json claimed the analyzer wrote, so the spec and the index disagreed while both looked correct.

Drops the read whose NAME is a concatenation. A `variable_reference` with no `word` of its own -- `$(PAPEROPT_$(PAPER))` parses as variable_reference -> concatenation -> word + variable_reference -- was read by looking for a `word` child, found none, and emitted nothing. The name is built at expand time so no file can declare it, but the READ is real: phpmyadmin/docs/Makefile declares PAPEROPT_a4 and PAPEROPT_letter and then reads `$(PAPEROPT_$(PAPER))`, so this edge is the only thing in the graph connecting those two declarations to the read that selects between them. Found when the corpus grew to 100 files and the differential reported 2 of these MISSING, with the oracle deriving them independently.

Relabels the computed-name read from `uses` to `references`. The lane's one rule is `references` iff THIS file declares the name, and no file can declare a name assembled at expand time, so `references` would publish a declaration that does not exist -- the same category error the lane already avoids for automatic variables, builtins and external prerequisites. The edge is kept, so only the label is wrong, which is exactly the shape a label-only gate cannot see.

Records the `word` half of a concatenated name instead of the whole computed name -- `FLAVOUR_` rather than `FLAVOUR_$(FLAV)`. The prefix appears nowhere in the file as a name, so the edge names a variable no declaration matches and the read that selects between FLAVOUR_a and FLAVOUR_b is lost. Same shape as the pre-existing `keep-dollar-wrapper-in-prerequisite` mutant, on the other half of the same expression.

Reverts MAKE-G1: `VPATH = src:include` is no longer modelled. VPATH is a GNU Make builtin whose value a makefile may set, exactly like CURDIR or MAKEFILE_LIST, and the sibling `vpath %.c src` directive has always been recorded -- so the two spellings of one feature were deliberately asymmetric, and the asymmetry cost a real edge: because VPATH was never declared, a read of it fell to `uses`, the class the lane reserves for names NOTHING can declare, even though this file is the thing that declares it.

Keeps the VPATH declaration but relabels the read of it from `references` to `uses` -- the exact split the lane exists to keep honest. `references` is emitted iff THIS file declares the name; `uses` carries a builtin / external / automatic class and asserts a declaration that does not exist. Only the label changes, which is the shape no count-based gate can see.

Invents a symbol for each search directory in a `VPATH =` value. `src`, `include` and `vendor` are PATHS the file looks in, not declarations it makes, and the strings appear in essentially every Makefile in existence as bare words -- so this floods the graph with path-shaped symbols and makes the completeness census report a declaration rate that is an artefact of a colon-separated value. A related mutant publishes `VPATH -> src` as a dependency, which is the category error the dangle adjudication exists to prevent.

Simulates the failure mode of a `.RECIPEPREFIX` patch that does not consume the prefix as its own token: the target is named `>build` instead of `build`. The prefix is a LINE prefix, never part of the name, so every reference and prerequisite keyed on the target silently stops matching.

Drops the second rule of the `.RECIPEPREFIX` fixture, which is the shape two rejected versions of the grammar patch actually produced: a comment between two rules ended the recipe `repeat` and the following rule was absorbed into the previous one, so `clean:` was published as a `recipe_line` inside `build`. A rule silently becoming part of the previous rule's recipe is the failure the fixture exists to catch, and the CORPUS COULD NOT SEE IT -- 0 of the 100 pinned files put a comment between two recipe lines. A four-line synthetic repro did.

Declares a symbol for the `.RECIPEPREFIX` setting. The directive configures HOW recipe lines begin; it declares no buildable object and no variable any rule can depend on, so a symbol for it would appear in a completeness census as a declaration the language does not have.

Publishes the dropped trailing recipe line's shell text as a symbol, which is what tree-sitter error recovery produces when the final recipe line has no terminating newline. The recipe line is not lost in make's model -- GNU Make 4.3 runs it -- so a symbol named after its command is a dependency the build file does not have. Found by make/recipe-eof-no-newline; the corpus cannot see it because 0 of the 100 pinned files lack a trailing newline.

Adds a `uses` edge from the target to the dropped trailing recipe line's command. Same root cause as the fabricated symbol above -- the final recipe line has no terminating newline -- and the more dangerous half: a target now depends on something it does not depend on.

Caught by markdown/code-block-site-identity's `expectSymbolCount { name: code_block.scala#2, equals: 1 }` and by markdown/table-structure's `forbidSymbols { Name/Meaning#2 }`.

REVERT: the heading-hierarchy edge is dropped whenever the two ends spell the same string, i.e. the self-edge filter is asked about NAMES rather than about identity. A `## Changelog` under a `# Changelog` is two distinct sites -- the child's id is qualified by its parent's -- so the containment is real and the edge must be published. Found by the differential rather than by the read, and found quietly: the tree oracle derives the edge from the grammar, the analyzer did not have it, and the kubernetes draw read MISSING=1 in about one draw in nine (`vendor/github.com/google/uuid/CHANGELOG.md`), which is the rate at which a reader writes a count off as sampling noise. Caught by markdown/heading-parent-name-collision, whose two `Changelog -> Changelog` rows and `Setup -> Setup` row cannot be satisfied by a name-keyed filter.

REVERT: a table column declares no symbol, while its `table_column` edge is still emitted -- the state in which the analyzer's own comment said 'a column is a site too' and the site never shipped. Measured after the repeat-site fix, over the same 120 files, 31 endpoints still named no symbol and every remaining one was a column. The edges survive this mutant on purpose: that is what made the defect invisible, because a count of relationships cannot tell an edge to nothing from an edge to something. Caught by markdown/table-structure's `isMarkdownTableColumn` assertions and its `Reading -> Reading` column edge.

REVERT: a same-document reference is published with its RAW FRAGMENT as the target, i.e. the state this round measured at 10,174 fragments in a 420-file draw, every one an edge to a name no symbol declared. A link writes a heading's ANCHOR and the lane published heading TEXT, so the two spellings could not meet: `## Install Now!` publishes as `Install Now!` and a link to it says `#install-now`, and nothing in the file is called `install-now`. 10,158 of those references now resolve and 16 name a heading that does not exist. The differential could not see it for the same reason it could not see MD-12: the oracle derived the same raw fragment, so the two agreed at 100% on a name neither published. Caught by markdown/internal-anchor-links' `forbidRelationships`, whose rows name the raw fragment specifically because an implementation that resolved nothing and one that resolved everything-but-wrote-the-fragment both look correct to a count.

MD-G1 REVERT: an INDENTED (four-space) code block publishes nothing, while the fenced form beside it publishes a per-site `function`. Measured with the block grammar over 1,138 pinned corpus files: 217 `indented_code_block` nodes, every one of them a node the grammar names. The gap originally recorded 2 sites, measured by a text heuristic; the grammar is 100x that, and most of the 217 are the wrapped continuation lines of deeply-nested list items, which CommonMark genuinely reads as indented code. So the revert deletes 217 symbols, which is why the symbol COUNT is the assertion here and not a name: a lane that published them under a different name would satisfy a name filter and still lose the construct. Caught by markdown/indented-code-block, whose expectSymbolCount totals 6 blocks across 3 sections and whose `Not a code block` forbid rows stop the fixture being satisfied by treating any indented line as code.
Drops MATLAB function_call relationships.
Drops nested declaration containment.
Drops class superclass relationships.
Drops field receiver/member construct metadata.

`type A = concept x of B` is filed as `extends` instead of `implements`. This is the neighbouring-type confusion question 4 asks about, and it is the exact mistake of routing the `of` clause through the nominal-inheritance pass: a concept is satisfied STRUCTURALLY and implicitly, there is no vtable and no nominal subtype relation in a refinement, so `extends` asserts a storage containment that does not exist. Caught by nim/concept's expectRelationships {implements, Addable -> Number} and, in the other direction, by its forbidRelationships {extends, target: Number}.

The `implements` family stops being emitted while the symbols stay `interface`. A concept that refines another contract declares that it INCLUDES that contract's operations, and nothing else in the payload records it — the visibility marker does not, the declared-type `references` edge does not. Dropping the family leaves the language's only interface relation invisible while every other signal still looks healthy. Caught by nim/concept's four expectRelationships rows.

`of Number, Container` yields only its FIRST entry. `refinement_list` is `sep1($.type_expression, ",")`, so a concept may name several contracts, and a reader that stops at one turns a refinement of two contracts into a claim about one — silently, and only for the multi-contract spelling. Caught by nim/concept's {implements, Both -> Container}, which has no sibling row that could satisfy it.

`of Source[T]` publishes the type ARGUMENT `T` instead of the refined contract `Source`. `refinement_list` is `sep1($.type_expression, ",")` and a generic instantiation is a `bracket_expression` whose FIRST named child is the constructor while its `argument_list` holds the type arguments, so a reader that takes the last name under the list lands on the argument. This is 2 of the family's 47 corpus edges — nimony's `tconceptinheritnotgeneric.nim:7 Bar = concept of Foo[T]` and `tconceptinvocationbody.nim:39 MutableIndexable*[T] = concept of Indexable[T]` — and it was unpinned until that repo entered the corpus on 2026-10-04. The edge it produces is a FABRICATION, not a mislabel: `T` is a generic parameter, it resolves at neither end, and `bb_impact` on it is wrong refactoring advice. This lane's own oracle made exactly this mistake on its first pass and the oracle cross-check caught it one round after the code was written. Caught by nim/concept's forbidRelationships {implements, Wrapped -> T}, whose sibling positive row {implements, Wrapped -> Source} has no other way to fail.

`type Cycle = concept of Cycle` publishes `Cycle implements Cycle`. A concept refining itself is not a relationship, and this is a REAL corpus file rather than a synthetic one: nimony/tests/nimony/concepts/tconceptcycle.nim is exactly that one line, and upstream ships tconceptcycle.msgs reading `Error: concept inheritance cycle detected`. The guard already exists for this family, on both spellings, but only the `is`-form half was pinned by a fixture — so a change that kept `r is Recursive` suppressed while dropping the `of`-form guard would have passed the suite. Caught by nim/concept's forbidRelationships {implements, from: Cycle}, which has no sibling row: `Cycle` refines nothing else.

Concept SATISFACTION is inferred and published: every ordinary object type in the file gets an `implements` edge to every concept it structurally matches. Nim has no syntax for satisfaction — it is the compiler's structural match against the concept body at instantiation time — so every one of these edges is fabricated, at confidence 0.5 where the analyzer knows it is guessing. A fabricated edge is counted `unexplained` by the oracle and poisons bb_graph/bb_impact, where a fake implementer becomes wrong refactoring advice. Caught by nim/concept's forbidRelationships {implements, from: Meters}: the fixture declares one plain object type next to eight concepts, so an inferred satisfaction edge has to name it and cannot.

`export M except a, b` publishes `a` and `b` as exported. `except` is the author saying those names do NOT leave the module, so this states the inverse of the construct, and it is the defect the pre-round reader actually had: it walked every identifier under `export_statement`. The form is real — nim/compiler/nifstreams.nim withholds nine names this way, and 9 of 155 corpus `export_statement` nodes carry an `except_clause`. Caught by nim/reexport's forbidRelationships {exports, target: helper} and {exports, target: another}, plus forbidExports on both names.

`export common_parser.Parser` publishes the endpoint as the WRITTEN form `common_parser.Parser` instead of the leaf `Parser`. The store resolves an endpoint by matching it against a symbol name, so the written form resolves at neither end while the lane's own symbols are all spelled `Parser` — the edge counts as resolved-looking and is not. Caught by nim/reexport's expectRelationships {exports, target: Parser} and its forbidExports {name: Parser} would not fire, but the relationship row cannot match a dotted endpoint.

Every `export` operand is put back into the importable-unit list, including the ones this file does not declare. That list is the index's provider set: giving a name two providers is how an importer's binding gets attributed to the wrong file. The re-export belongs on the RELATIONSHIP, which says 'this module hands this name onward' and is true whoever declares it. Caught by nim/reexport's forbidExports {name: foo}, {name: Parser}, {name: strutils}, {name: std/os}.

The regression that shipped in the first version of the `implements` reader: `childForFieldName("refines")` returns the `refinement_list` node ITSELF, and the reader looked for a CHILD of that type instead. Every file therefore produced zero refinements while the concept was still published as `interface`, so every other signal looked healthy and the whole `implements` family read zero occurrences on a construct the corpus and the fixtures both spell correctly. This mutant reproduces it exactly — the edges go, the symbols stay. Caught by nim/concept's four expectRelationships rows, and it is the reason the field-shape fact now has one function (`refinementListOf`) read by both consumers rather than one per consumer.

The `*` visibility marker is published a second time as an `exports` EDGE. Visibility is already carried — `visibility: "public"` plus `metadata.exported`, persisted into brain_symbol.visibility and read by gravity (28,900 exported_symbol nodes in 1,335 corpus files) — so the extra graph restates a fact at ~17.6% payload growth (163,960 edges measured before) for no query a reader could not already ask. Caught by nim/reexport's forbidRelationships {exports, target: visible}: the fixture declares `proc visible*()` and never exports it by statement.

A NAMED nested routine stops being published, which is the exact defect this lane fixed: 653 `calls` edges over 4,555 corpus files named a declaration the parse tree carried and the run published nowhere, because a `calls` EDGE was emitted while its far end had no symbol. The analyzer is a per-file walker with no second pass, so the regression is invisible in any edge count — only the symbol is missing. Caught by nim/nested's expectSymbols {recentlyOpenedAdd, scope: closeTab} and by its expectRelationships {contains, closeTab -> recentlyOpenedAdd}.

The nested routine keeps its symbol but loses `scope`, so it reads as a module procedure. The lua lane measured why this is a real defect and not cosmetics: `scope` is what a consumer reads to decide where a symbol belongs, and a closure declared inside `closeTab` does not belong to the file's module scope. It also breaks the `qualifiedName` the worker derives from `scope`, so `closeTab.recentlyOpenedAdd` stops resolving for the incoming walk. Caught by nim/nested's expectSymbols scope assertion.

A `runnableExamples` block's VALUE declarations are published as module symbols. `var base: Base = Sub1()` is a local of the example unit exactly as `var` in a routine body is a local of that routine, so this is `LocalsAreNotSymbols` violated in the opposite direction from the nested-routine fix — the two must be fixed together or the first fix reintroduces the second defect. Caught by nim/nested's forbidSymbols {exampleOnlyLocal}, a name the fixture declares nowhere else so the forbid cannot be satisfied by a coincidence.

The `runnableExamples:` doc pragma is published as a `calls` edge. This is the fabrication rule's cheapest available instance: the grammar parses the whole example as the call's `argument_list`, so the call branch fires on a keyword, and the edge lands on an identifier no Nim program can call — a name the graph can never resolve. Measured before the fix: 24 such frames in nim/lib/system.nim alone. Caught by nim/nested's forbidRelationships {calls, describe -> runnableExamples}.

A method stops publishing `qualifiedName`, so every `overrides` endpoint — which is receiver-qualified (`Rect.describe`) because the bare name cannot address either end — fails to resolve for the incoming walk. Measured with `script/m14/incoming-check.ts` on nim/lib/pure (105 files, 6,638 symbols) before the fix: 14 of 14 `overrides` edges reported as UNRESOLVED targets, every one a correct edge. The worker's `qualifiedName` fallback cannot recover it, because a method's owner is `ownerName`, not `scope`. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {describe, meta.fqn: Shape.describe}. The pin is on `meta.fqn` rather than on `qualifiedName` because run-fixtures.ts cannot assert the latter — it is missing from CONSTRAINT_KEY_ALLOWLIST, so a row carrying it is reported as an INERT assertion. `pool-worker.ts:870` reads `s.qualifiedName || s.metadata?.fqn`, so both carry the same fact and the metadata one is the assertable channel.

A parenless UFCS call of a NESTED routine stops being emitted. `s.trimmed` invokes `trimmed(s)` with no parentheses and no call node, so the callee is a member leaf and the analyzer has to decide it is a callable by name. Testing only the module-scope set loses it, because nested routines are deliberately kept out of that set. Found by script/m14/nim-truth-oracle.ts: one unexplained `calls` edge on the 400-file sample, at nim/lib/packages/docutils/rst.nim:3493 where `rmSpaces` is declared at :3491 inside `proc dirImportdoc`. An analyzer that reads only its own metadata would have agreed with itself and reported nothing. Caught by nim/nested's forbidRelationships {uses, strip -> trimmed} — a mutant that reclassified the call as a read is caught by the same pin, because the shape is what is being asserted.

The bare-`case` guard stops applying, and the slot's borrowed constructor is published again as a field of the owning type with a `contains` edge to it. This is the defect itself, reproduced as a transform so the fixture is proved able to catch it. Caught by nim/bare-case's forbidSymbols {AddOpr, SubOpr, None, Some, float, Circle, Value} and its four forbidRelationships `contains` rows.

A `.nim` file stops publishing the MODULE it defines, so every `imports` edge names a module that exists nowhere in the symbol set. This is not a resolution failure — there is no candidate to fail to find — and the store cannot rescue it: the insert-time resolver matches `brain_symbol.name` (parallel-indexer.ts:2239), the three post-pass strategies match a bare name, a `qualified_name`, or everything after the first `.` of a dotted target (:3755-3774), and `std/assertions` is none of those; the fourth, `resolveImportTargets`, is scoped to the `<module>:<item>` form javascript/typescript/python emit and nim never reaches it. MEASURED with production `parseFile` over the 6,063-file corpus (validation/m14/fixtures/nim/census.ts): `imports` resolved on 37.1% of 13,364 edges before the module pass and 92.0% of 13,365 after it. Caught by nim/module-target's expectSymbols {module-target, kind: module}. The mutant is kept separate from the target-normalisation mutant below because dropping the symbol while keeping the normalised target leaves the edge pointing at a name that exists, which a target-only fixture would not notice is wrong.

The `imports` target goes back to the module path AS WRITTEN while the module symbol stays published. The two halves drifted apart in the first place, which is why this is expressible as its own mutant: the emitter wrote the path `parseModuleExpression` returned and the publisher wrote the file's basename, and no test compared them. `import std/os` then targets `std/os`, which no symbol carries, and `import ./helpers` targets `./helpers`. Both were CORRECT for the corpus by accident and wrong for the graph. Caught by nim/module-target's three forbidRelationships rows — {imports, std/os}, {imports, std/private/globs}, {imports, ../shared} — and by nim/contract's five retargeted `imports` rows, whose `meta.nimModulePath` pins the written path separately from the target so the two cannot be confused again. Verified by hand before registration: reverting the three target sites made nim/module-target and nim/contract FAIL (10 pass / 2 fail) with all three forbid rows firing.

The `std/` prefix stops being recognised, so every standard-library import is emitted indistinguishably from a local one. The edges are still correct and still resolve where the corpus contains the module — this removes a LABEL, not an edge, which is exactly why it needs its own pin: the resolution census is blind to it. `nim/module-target` pins `meta.nimStdlibModule: true` on the three `std/` rows (`os`, `strutils`, `globs`).

The marker is applied to EVERY `imports` edge, which is the fabrication this workstream calls its most expensive mistake: it asserts that a local module is part of the standard library. `import ../shared` and `import ./helpers` would both be marked, and 309 of the 485 unbindable corpus edges are BARE names — a local module, a `lib/pure` module (`import re`) and a typo are the same string in one file and nothing per-file separates them. Caught by nim/module-target's `meta.nimStdlibModule: null` row on the `../shared` edge, which the runner reads as "must not carry this key". The first version of this mutant was verified by hand before registration: marking every import made nim/module-target FAIL on that row alone.

A relative import publishes no edge — the replacement for the disarmed `nim/relative-import-lost`. The pre-fix rule only read the infix path shape, so the leading `./` — a PREFIX operator, not a path segment — made every `import ./sibling` vanish, and a three-file module whose files all import each other relatively measured 0 imports. Selected on `meta.nimModulePath`, which keeps the written `./helpers` and `../shared` the old filter looked for, while the target is the module name. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {imports -> helpers} and {imports -> shared}, and by nim/module-target's {imports -> shared} row.

A path deeper than two segments publishes no edge — the replacement for the disarmed `nim/deep-import-path-lost`. The grammar models the separator as a NAMED `operator` node whose text is the whole token (`/`, or `/../` fused with a parent hop), so `op.type` is never `/` and an identifier/identifier test never matched: 171 deep-path imports across 141 corpus files and 434 multi-segment relative imports across 299 files published nothing, and because the whole path vanished there was no dangling target to surface it. Caught by nim/contract's expectImports {module: std/private/globs} AND its expectRelationships sibling {imports -> globs} — both, because the imports half and the edge half fail independently and pinning only one leaves the other unguarded.

`import std/[os, strutils]` publishes ONE edge for the whole list instead of one per element, so a two-module import becomes a single dependency on a name no file has — the replacement for the disarmed `nim/module-list-collapsed-to-one-edge`, which matched the old target strings `std/os`/`std/strutils` and therefore matched nothing once the targets became `os`/`strutils`. Caught by nim/module-target's two rows for `os` and `strutils` and nim/contract's expectImports {module: std/os} + {module: std/strutils}: one pin alone would pass, which is why both are there.

A from-import keeps its `imports[]` row and loses only its `imports` EDGE — the half of `nim/cross-file-macro-called-without-an-import` that the target normalisation disarmed, isolated so it can be caught on its own. Its shared twin still passes because its `imports[].module` half fires; this one fires only the dead half, and before this entry it was the state of the shared mutant: a guard whose edge clause could not fail. A file-dependency consumer reads the EDGE, so an imports row with no edge is exactly the invisible-dependency defect the family `imports` type exists to prevent. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {imports -> mac} and nim/module-target's four rows.

The member-access branch stops publishing the RECEIVER — `meta.fieldAccessExpression` goes from "c.id" to absent — while the edge itself still targets the bare `id`. Nothing else changes: same edge, same target, same confidence, one metadata key gone. Caught by nim/field-receiver's three expectRelationships rows, each of which pins `meta.fieldAccessExpression`. This mutant exists because of what it would cost SILENTLY. `field-type-ceiling.mts` derives its whole answer from that key — it is what makes `Character.id` derivable without an import graph — so if the key stopped being published the ceiling would read 0 and the documented decision not to build the rule would still be quoted as evidence. A null ceiling and a worthless ceiling are indistinguishable in the artifact, and only one of them is a statement about Nim. The fixture is what distinguishes them.

`readParameters` keeps the parameter NAME and drops its declared TYPE, so `c` arrives as a parameter with no type where the source read `c: Character`. The member-access edge is untouched and still carries `fieldAccessExpression: "c.id"`. Caught by nim/field-receiver's expectParameters rows for charToResp and shipToResp, which pin both name and type. It is the second of the two premises the B1 ambiguity ceiling rests on, and the cheaper of the two to lose without noticing: without a parameter type there is no qualifier to apply, so `field-type-ceiling.mts` would fall from 42 file-unique candidates to 9 rejected at "parameter has no declared type" — and a ceiling that reads 0 looks exactly like a ceiling that measured 0.

the FILE-LOCAL PRAGMA-TEMPLATE RESOLUTION IS REVERTED: a declaration's `{.myMarker.}` is left as symbol metadata and no `decorates` row is published. This is the exact regression the ruling would have made permanent — the lane planned to rule the type ontological and the census's 294 applied callables in pragma positions falsified that ruling — so the positive half of nim/pragma-decorates must catch it. WITHOUT this mutant the entire emission could be deleted and the suite would stay green, which is the failure mode the fleet keeps paying for.

the discriminator is dropped and EVERY declaration-owned pragma name becomes a `decorates` row — so `{.inline.}` decorates the proc that carries it. This is the partial fix that is WORSE than the bug it replaces: it would turn the 0.9 % applied-callable class into the full 33,266-name pragma population and make the `decorates` cell mean nothing. Caught by nim/pragma-decorates' forbid half (no decorates target `inline`, no decorates from `directiveOnly`), which is why the negative half exists at all.

`type C = ref object` goes back to a bare `type`. The pre-fix rule read the `object` keyword and missed the `ref_type` wrapper, so every identity-bearing class in the language — the shape inheritance and dynamic dispatch exist for — was published as a type-level name. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Shape, class} and {Rect, class}.

The mirror of the mutant above, and the one that keeps the first honest: over-applying `ref` would turn a copying `object` into a class. `Builder` and `Registry` are plain `object`s. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Builder, struct} and {Registry, struct}.

`type Addable = concept` goes back to a `type`. A concept is the language's structural interface — satisfied by implicit dispatch, no nominal subtype anywhere — which is exactly what SymbolKind.Interface means in this codebase. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Addable, interface}.
`type Color = enum` goes back to a `type`, losing the enum kind. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Color, enum}.

Enum members stop being symbols. `Red`, `Green` and `Blue` are the values code actually compares on, and a variant object's `of Red:` discriminates on them. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Red/Green/Blue, enum_member}.

Object fields stop being symbols, so every property access in the language has no declaration to resolve to. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {name, property}, {w, property} and the rest of the eight.

`iterator countUp` goes back to a macro. An iterator is callable and is reached by `for … in countUp(3)`, so classifying it as a macro breaks the one symbol kind that has a call syntax of its own. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {countUp, function}.

`template twice` goes back to a function. A template is hygienic and is expanded before name resolution, so it is not a callable value; the macro kind is what keeps it out of the call graph as a runtime edge. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {twice, macro}.

`method describe` goes back to a function, which costs the receiver: the override edge is owner-qualified (`Rect.describe -> Shape.describe`) and a method is the only kind that carries one. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {describe, method} and by the overrides pin that names `Rect.describe`.

A file-scope `let` goes back to a `constant`. Nim's `let` is a single immutable binding and `const` is compile-time; collapsing them loses the distinction that tells a reader whether a value exists at runtime. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Greeting, variable}.
A file-scope `const` goes back to a `variable` — the same collapse from the other side, so the pair cannot both pass by being quiet. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {MaxItems, constant}.

`type Pair = tuple[x, y: int]` goes back to a `type`. A tuple type has fields exactly as an object does, and the field names are destructurable (`let (a, b) = pair`), so the struct kind is what lets `x`/`y` be properties. Caught by nim/contract's expectSymbols {Pair, struct}.

`type Registry*[T] = object` publishes `T` as a type symbol. A generic parameter is bound by the declaration, not declared by it, so `T` is not something the index can resolve a reference to. Caught by nim/contract's forbidSymbols {T, type}.

Import edges stop being emitted at all, which empties the module dependency graph — the one relationship an LSP "what does this file depend on" query cannot answer without. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {imports, (global) -> std/os} and the five sibling import pins.

Import edges come back as `references`. This is the defect the differential could not see: the oracle and the analyzer agreed, both were 0-unexplained, and every NIM dependency edge was still invisible to the reader that looks at relationship_type IN ('imports','exports'). Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {type: imports, (global) -> ./mac}.

A relative import publishes no edge. The pre-fix rule only read the infix path shape, and the leading `./` is a PREFIX operator, so every `import ./sibling` in a module vanished — measured 0 imports for a three-file module whose files all import each other relatively, while the same analyzer returned imports for `import std/os`. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {imports, -> ./helpers} and {imports, -> ../shared}.

A path deeper than two segments publishes no edge. The grammar models the separator as a NAMED `operator` node whose text is the whole token (`/`, or `/../` fused with a parent hop), so `op.type` is never `/` and the pre-fix identifier/identifier test never matched: 171 deep-path imports across 141 corpus files and 434 multi-segment relative imports across 299 files published nothing, and because the whole path vanished there was no dangling target to surface it. Caught by nim/contract's expectImports {module: std/private/specialpaths} and its expectRelationships sibling.

`import std/[os, strutils]` publishes ONE edge for the whole list instead of one per element, so a two-module import becomes a single dependency on a name no file has. Caught by nim/contract's expectImports {module: std/os} AND {module: std/strutils} — one pin alone would pass, which is why both are there.

`from ./nativesettings import …` publishes the target `nativesettings` while `import ./configure` publishes `./configure`: two spellings for one module in one graph, from two path readers inside one analyzer. Found by the differential on prologue's application.nim, three edges disagreeing in both directions. Caught by nim/contract's expectImports {module: ./macros, meta.nimFromImport} and its expectRelationships sibling.

Ownership edges stop being emitted, so no symbol has a parent and every method and field is an orphan in the graph. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {contains, Shape -> name} and {contains, Color -> Red}.

Call edges stop being emitted. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {calls, exercise -> makeRect} and {calls, build -> join} — the second is a UFCS call, so the pair also pins that `b.parts.join(",")` has no dot-call node and the member leaf is the callee.

Value-read edges stop being emitted. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {uses, exercise -> Greeting} and {uses, build -> parts} — the second is the member leaf of a UFCS read, which is a `uses` edge distinct from the `calls` edge on the same expression.
Declared-type edges stop being emitted, so a signature no longer states what it accepts. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {references, area -> Rect} and {references, exercise -> Builder}.
Object construction stops being an `instantiates` edge. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {instantiates, makeRect -> Rect}.
Inheritance edges stop being emitted. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {extends, Rect -> Shape}.
Override edges stop being emitted, so a derived method reads as a new method rather than a replacement. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {overrides, Rect.describe -> Shape.describe}.

An override target goes back to the BARE method name, so `Rect.describe` and `Shape.describe` become the same target and the edge says a method overrides itself. Receiver qualification is the only thing that distinguishes an override from a same-named sibling. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {overrides, from: Rect.describe} — the pin is on the SOURCE spelling for exactly this reason.

`Rect(name: "r", …)` publishes `uses makeRect -> name`, i.e. a read of the field `name` that never happens. Nim has no ternary, so `x: value` in an expression only ever names a field of a construction or a variant branch — it never reads one. The edge resolves to a real symbol, so no dangling check could ever catch it. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {uses, target: name}.

A destructuring binding never enters its scope frame, so a later read of that name is attributed to a same-named field elsewhere in the file. `let (_, name, _) = splitFile(f)` is a tuple_deconstruct_declaration WRAPPING its bindings, and the pre-fix binder took only children typed symbol_declaration, so the whole node was skipped. Measured on pixie: `name` was unbound, and the read at `images.add((name, image))` was published as `uses renderEmojiSet -> name`, pointing at a struct property declared 26 lines earlier and unrelated to the binding. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {uses, from: stemOf, target: fileStem}, which is only a real assertion because the paired expectSymbols {fileStem, property} pins that the field exists — otherwise a fix that deleted the field would satisfy the forbid vacuously.

A call's callee is published as a `uses` read as well as a `calls` edge, so one call site produces two edges to one target. The pre-fix rule ran the bare-identifier read pass without excluding the callee subtree. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {uses, target: makeRect} — the callee is in the symbols, so the read pass could have claimed it.

The left side of an assignment is published as a value read. `written = b.parts.len` would then carry a `uses build -> written` edge where the language has one write and one read of something else. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {uses, from: build, target: written} — the pin has to be on the SOURCE because a target-only pin would also forbid the legitimate reads of `written` elsewhere in the file.

`echo`, `discard` and the numeric conversions become call targets. These are compiler builtins and keywords, and an edge to them is a dependency on a name no file declares — the shape the house precedent suppresses for java's println and groovy's printf. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {calls, target: echo}, {calls, target: discard} and {calls, target: float}.
`_` — the blank identifier, which appears in every destructuring pattern and every `proc f(_: int)` signature — is published as a variable. Caught by nim/contract's forbidSymbols {_, variable}.

Relationships stop carrying a line at all. A relationship with no line cannot be shown in a file, and the seam gate's out-of-range check has nothing to check. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships line_number pins on an import, a contains, an overrides and a uses edge — four different name sites, because a rule that anchored every edge to one node's line would satisfy a single pin.

An import's line becomes the line of the `import` KEYWORD rather than of the module token. A multi-line `import` puts the paths on later lines than the keyword, so this points a reader at the wrong line for every such edge — and the corpus's own `nim/compiler/nimsets.nim` is the example: `import` on line 12, `ast, astalgo, …` on line 13. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {imports, -> ../shared, line_number} on a `from` import whose keyword and operand are on the same line but whose OPERAND is the evidence.

Every edge is stamped `evidenceClass: "structural"`, erasing the distinction the taxonomy depends on: ownership and inheritance are structural facts, while a read, a call and a construction are contextual, a type name reached through a qualifier is reference_qualified, and a type resolved through an import graph is import_based. A flat tier makes a guess look like a fact. Caught by nim/contract's four meta.evidenceClass pins, including two DIFFERENT tiers on the SAME kind (references: area->Rect reference_qualified, makeRect->Rect import_based).

Every symbol's cyclomatic complexity becomes 1 — the shape a complexity counter lands in when its decision-point node types do not match the grammar, which is a real failure mode found in other lanes (perl's counter was 1 for almost every file because six node-type literals were dead). Caught by nim/contract's expectComplexity {exercise, equals 3} and {countUp, equals 2}.

Documentation comments stop reaching the symbol. Nim's `##` doc comment is how a proc documents its contract, and losing it is invisible in a symbol count. Caught by nim/contract's expectDocstrings on `area`, whose `## Area of a rectangle.` is the fixture's only doc comment.

Pragmas stop being published as decorators. `{.inline.}` is a calling-convention contract and `{.base.}` is the method-dispatch marker that tells a reader which `describe` is the root of the override chain — losing it makes the override edge unexplainable from the symbol alone. Caught by nim/contract's expectDecorators pinning `inline` on `area` and `base` on `describe`.

A macro imported from another file stops publishing its import, leaving `discard retTrue()` calling a name the file never declares — a dangling edge, and the reason nim/contract forbids `retTrue` as a SYMBOL in the first place. The call edge itself is legitimate (the macro really is called); the mutant removes the edge that explains where it came from. Caught by nim/contract's expectImports {module: ./mac, meta.nimFromImport} together with its forbidSymbols {retTrue, function} — the pair, because either alone would pass.

A PARENLESS UFCS member call stops being a call: `let s = b.build` and `r.describe` are `build(b)` and `describe(r)` written with no parentheses and no call node, so the member-leaf pass had no callee branch and published nothing. Found by the M12 ground truth — its audit asserted the row by reading the source, which is the one move an oracle that mirrors the analyzer cannot make, because the differential's oracle omitted it too and the lane reported 0% unexplained with both wrong in the same direction. Caught by nim/contract's expectRelationships {calls, exercise -> build}.

A concept stops being a scope frame, so its formal parameter becomes unbound and the reads in its body are published as file-scope value reads: `type Addable = concept x` / `(x + x) is SomeNumber` produced `uses (global) -> x`. A concept parameter is the one formal parameter in Nim written with no symbol_declaration wrapper and no type annotation, so no other rule caught it. Found by the M12 ground truth as its single false positive at precision 0.990. Caught by nim/contract's forbidRelationships {uses, (global) -> x}.

A method stops declaring `ownerName`, i.e. it stops being OWNED by its receiver type. That one field is the family standard for ownership, and dropping it silently disabled three things at once: the `contains` edge from the receiver to the method, the store's ownership binding, and the project-wide override companion index — which is why cross-file override resolution could not work no matter what the override pass did. The companion came back EMPTY for a file whose base class declared a method. Caught by nim/extbase's expectSymbols {render, method, ownerName: ExtBase} and its expectRelationships {contains, ExtBase -> render}; the symbol pin is listed first because the edge alone would also be satisfied by a hardcoded owner.

M59.A7 regression: every relationship's `line_number` is dropped again — this is the lane's state at HEAD before the round (0 of 21,591 edges lined, which is why the `lines` cell read `fail`), and the line pins die in objc/edges-and-patterns, objc/selector-identity and objc/payload-and-complexity
M59.A7 regression: every claimed line shifts by one (the 0/1-base confusion whose line the equivalence probe refuses) — the line pins die, and the near-miss forbids are the second net

M59.A7 regression, the near-miss the fixtures FORBID: a `contains` row carries the CONTAINER's declaration line instead of the member's. This is the spelling that would have looked plausible here (the lane symbolizes a method at its implementation, so the container's line is the one a careless stamp would reach for), and only the member-name pins and their forbids can see it — a row whose line names `@interface Counter` still confirms a name that IS on that line

R8 (M60) regression: the emitted array goes back to the SET'S INSERTION ORDER, which is the pre-fix observable — the analyzer published `[...frameworks]` and picked `[...frameworks][0]`, so the payload was the order the `#import` statements happened to be walked in. Caught by objc/framework-surface-pins, which imports Foundation and Cocoa FIRST and pins [UIKit, AppKit, Cocoa, Foundation] with UIKit as the primary pick: the mutant emits [Foundation, Cocoa, AppKit, UIKit] and picks Foundation — the base library every Objective-C file imports, reported as the primary framework of a UIKit view.

R8 (M60) regression: the lane goes back to publishing `detectedFrameworks` and a primary pick and NOTHING ELSE — the state the census registered as missing-contract-key and the runtime half measured on 7 of 7 detecting files over 153 real corpus files. `frameworkPatterns` is not a redundant copy of detection: it says what was observed and therefore why the framework is claimed. Caught by objc/framework-surface-pins' frameworkPatterns metadata pin, and by the R8 runtime probe's A7 assertion — which exists because this exact shape measured CLEAN before it was added.

PERL-1 REVERT: a dependency the file does not declare publishes no reading again — the pre-fix state, where the whole population read 10,096 edges and 9,435 ambiguous/unresolved with ZERO verified claims: `use strict` (328), `use Test::More` (267), `is(…)` (206), `plan(…)` (175), `ok(…)` (118) all named a dependency and said nothing. Keyed on the row's own claim keys (`externalVia: use|call`, `externalReason: module-namespace`), not on a fixture name. Caught by perl/external-deps-perl1's four positive rows.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `imports` EDGE, not the `imports` payload. The lane recorded every module load as an `ImportInfo` row and ZERO relationships, and payload is not an edge — `parallel-indexer` writes `result.imports` into the `brain_import` TABLE and only `result.relationships` into `brain_relationship`, which is the table `bb_graph` reads. So for perl the module dependency graph had no edges to traverse: a file's dependencies existed and nothing could ask for them. Measured on mojo: 1,287 `imports` edges over 274 files. Caught by perl/ontology-imports, which pins seven of them including the heritage pragma, the runtime `require` and the in-sub-body `use`.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `exports` EDGE. Same shape as the imports defect on the other half of the module surface — 2,170 export names as `ExportInfo` payload, zero relationships — and `bb_graph --mode usages` reads `relationship_type IN ('imports','exports')`, so a perl module's exported API was in the store and in no graph. Measured on mojo: 84 `exports` edges over 274 files. Caught by perl/ontology-exports, which pins all three Exporter surfaces: `@EXPORT`, the optional `@EXPORT_OK`, and the `%EXPORT_TAGS` KEYS.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `uses` EDGE. A CODE-SLOT REFERENCE (`\&sub`, `\&Class::method`) and a qualified VARIABLE READ (`$Foo::bar`) both name a declaration the file depends on and invoke nothing — go's definition of the label. The pre-fix lane emitted exactly ONE such edge on mojo's first 40 files, the unqualified `\&SIGINT`, so the count read as a working rule rather than as a rule that could only fire on the one shape that had no `::`. Measured: 54 `uses` edges on mojo's 274 files after the fix. Caught by perl/ontology-uses.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `references` EDGE, and perl's declared-TYPE positions. `bless $r, 'Class'` binds a reference to a named class — the analogue of java's `instanceof` — and `$o->isa('C')`, `$o->DOES('R')` and `ref($x) eq 'C'` test one. None can be a `calls` edge: `bless`, `ref` and `isa` are in `PERL_BUILTINS` and are suppressed as call targets. Measured on mojo: 19 `references` edges over 274 files. Caught by perl/ontology-references, which pins all four constructs and forbids six fabrications.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `Owner.member` rewrite of a `uses` target, which was DEAD BY CONSTRUCTION. `qualifiedTarget` rewrote `\&Mojo::Util::decode` to `Util.decode`, and `isWrittenCalleeName` refuses a `.` — so the rewrite could only ever produce a target the very next line rejected. Every qualified perl name in the corpus was therefore DROPPED, and because the edge was dropped rather than published wrong, no count, no differential row and no fixture could see it: the lane reported 1 `uses` edge and read that as a working rule. The independent oracle reproduced the same `.decode` string verbatim, which is the cleanest statement available of what a shared convention is worth — two implementations agreeing on a question about SPELLING, where the question was never about the grammar. Caught by perl/ontology-uses, whose target rows are the names AS WRITTEN and whose forbid rows name the rewrite's output.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the qualified-VARIABLE-READ branch tested the OWNER half WITH its trailing `::`, and `isWrittenPackageName("Config::")` is false by construction — a package name that ends where a segment must begin is not one. So `$Config::SSL_ERROR`, `@Some::Module::LIST` and `%Foo::Bar::MAP` produced no edge at all. Same shape of error as the rewrite above, one function over, and it was equally invisible: `uses` measured 1 edge and the one was the unqualified `\&SIGINT`. Caught by perl/ontology-uses, whose three `qualified-variable-read` rows carry the full qualification.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: `arguments` is a SINGLE field on an `ambiguous_function_call_expression`, so `bless $self, 'Class'` hands the literal reader one `list_expression` node — not a literal — and `writtenLiteralName` returns undefined for it. The construct the whole `references` label rests on produced NO edge. The discriminant is not subtle; it is that `bless` is a builtin and is suppressed as a call target, so there was no other edge for the file to carry and no count anywhere that moved. Caught by perl/ontology-references, whose first row is the `bless` literal.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: a code-slot REFERENCE written where the grammar types a CALL. `defined &builtin::is_bool` parses as `func1op_call_expression(defined, function_call_expression(&builtin::is_bool))` — there is no `refgen_expression` in it at all, so a `refgen_expression`-only branch cannot see perl's most idiomatic conditional probe. The discriminator is the ARGUMENT LIST and never the leading `&`, because `&foo(@args)` is perl's explicit-call syntax; suppressing on the `&` alone cost 323 truth rows across perl5 when the lane tried it the other way. Caught by perl/ontology-uses, whose third row is a bare `&` reference and whose last forbid row is the same spelling WITH an argument list.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: a perl `use` is LEXICALLY SCOPED, so a pragma is very often written inside a sub body — mojo's lib/Mojo/Util.pm says `use integer;` at lines 263, 296 and 492, all inside subs, and lib/Mojo/Base.pm does `require Mojo::Promise;` inside a sub. Reading either construct only at file scope publishes a dependency graph with those loads missing, and the numbers barely move (4 of 253 on mojo's 60-file draw), which is how it stayed invisible. Caught by perl/ontology-imports, whose `Runtime::Inside` and `integer` rows are both inside sub bodies.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: a PRAGMA is emitted as an `imports` edge and TAGGED (`meta.isPragma`) rather than dropped. `strict` in particular is a hard prerequisite for the file to compile at all, each pragma is a real module the file genuinely loads, and — the load-bearing reason — the `ImportInfo` PAYLOAD already carries every `use`, so an edge set that quietly omitted the pragmas would disagree with the payload it is derived from. Two answers to one question is the defect the ontology workstream is about. A consumer that wants the module graph without pragmas reads `isPragma`, which is one column rather than a second, disagreeing answer. Caught by perl/ontology-imports, whose `strict` and `integer` rows pin `meta.isPragma: true`.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: `use 5.010` and `require 5.010` are a LANGUAGE VERSION requirement — `require_version_expression` is a different node type, and the `use` form goes to `metadata.perlVersion` — and neither becomes an `imports` edge. An import named `5.010` puts a fake module in the dependency graph and in every unused-import report. Caught by perl/ontology-imports, whose forbid rows name `5.010` on both the payload and the edge.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: `ref($x) eq 'ARRAY'` names perl's OWN type vocabulary, not a class, and there is no declaration anywhere named `ARRAY`. Measured on mojo: `ref(...) eq 'X'` occurs 67 times and 66 of them are `ARRAY` (30), `HASH` (23) or `CODE` (13); exactly one is a class. A rule written from the SHAPE rather than the ROLE would therefore have been 98.5% fabricated — the same failure the ontology gate's own header records for a bash probe that matched `class voice` inside a telnet IAC word list. The internal names are DERIVED, not hand-listed, the same way `PERL_BUILTINS` is. Caught by perl/ontology-references, whose `ARRAY` and `HASH` forbid rows are the control.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: `$obj->isa('My::Class')` invokes `isa` — a UNIVERSAL builtin no project declares — and it NAMES `My::Class`, which is a `references` edge. The pre-fix lane produced `calls -> isa`, naming a method nothing defines. Measured on mojo's first 40 files: 22 `calls -> isa` edges, and all 22 are `isa`. `DOES` is deliberately NOT in the same class: Moose::Object declares it, so a class really can override it and the `calls` edge is true — which is why the rule tests the METHOD name, never the shape of the edge. Caught by perl/ontology-references, whose last forbid row is `calls -> isa`.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: a class name that is COMPUTED is not a name. `bless $self, $class` is perl's commonest `bless` and names a variable; `"${class}::ISA"` computes its package half at runtime; `$obj->isa($class)` names a variable. A target that is not written cannot be verified, so publishing one is a fabricated claim rather than a weak one — and a fabricated edge is counted as `unexplained` and poisons `bb_graph`, `bb_impact` and `bb_migrate`. The internal-ref-type list is DERIVED from what a perl 5.34 interpreter itself prints for an unblessed reference, not hand-listed. Caught by perl/ontology-references, whose three computed-name forbid rows are the control.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: a role composition is a NAME LIST, and Moose/Moo write it in four shapes that look alike. Reading every word of the argument list published the fat-comma SLOT names as roles. Measured on Moose-2.4000: `t/roles/role_conflict_detection.t:139` produced `implements My::Test8 -> -alias` and `t/roles/more_alias_and_exclude.t:47` produced `-> excludes`, beside the real roles; and the fat-comma SPECIFICATION form (`with 'A' => {...}, 'B' => {...}`) put the roles in the KEYS with the modifiers one level deeper in the values. This is PERL-MR4's rule — a fat-comma key names a SLOT, not a declaration — stated for composition, and the independent oracle made the SAME mistake before the fix, which is why no differential could see it. Caught by perl/ontology-composition, whose six forbid rows are the modifier names.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: `with qw(RoleA RoleB)` and `extends qw(BaseA BaseB)` are ONE `quoted_word_list` node, so reading only its first word published the first role or base and dropped the rest. Measured on moo: 6 of 94 `implements` rows and 5 of 109 `extends` rows over 142 files, every one a real composition the file writes. Caught by perl/ontology-composition, whose `Role::Two` row is the second name of the same node on the same line.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: a `has` SPECIFICATION's fat-comma keys are OPTION names, not attributes. `has $_ => (@params, clearer => 1, predicate => 1)` published a `property` symbol and a `contains` edge named `clearer` — measured on moo `t/accessor-pred-clear.t:13`. The same reader also TRUNCATED a name that is not an identifier: `has 'has spaces'` became the property `has`, which is worse than publishing nothing because `has` is a real perl function and a `bb_impact` on it reaches every Moose class (measured on Moose-2.4000 `t/attributes/non_alpha_attr_names.t:25`, the file that exists to test that name). Caught by perl/ontology-composition, whose `has spaces` row pins the verbatim name and whose forbid rows name the option keys.

PERL-ONTOLOGY: the `use_statement` case ended in `return`, which skips the CHILD WALK — and a `use` statement can carry a declaration in its argument list. `use if (not our $__mx_is_compiled), 'Moose::Meta::Class'` is Moose's conditional-load idiom; measured on Moose-2.4000 `lib/Moose/Object.pm:15-16`, both `our` globals were absent from the symbol table, so nothing that reads `__mx_is_compiled` could find it. The identical early return had already cost this lane's ORACLE 47 inheritance rows on mojo in an earlier wave, and the lane's own truth module documents it. A `break` is the fix and it moves nothing else: the fixture suite is unchanged. Caught by perl/ontology-imports, whose `Runtime::Inside` row is a `require` reached only because the walk descends.

PERL-ONTOLOGY, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: a published call TARGET carries no sigil. `&use_module('X')` is perl's EXPLICIT-CALL syntax, so the edge is right — but a target spelled `&use_module` names a symbol no declaration carries and no resolver can match. Measured on Moose-2.4000 `lib/Moose/Util.pm`: 2 edges at lines 147 and 349. The `&` is stripped AFTER the two tests that need the source spelling (the builtin probe and `hasArgumentSyntax`), because both are about how the file wrote it. Caught by the differential rather than by a fixture, which is stated here rather than implied: this class has no fixture because no perl fixture in the lane calls a sub through `&`.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: `require` with a FILENAME specifier. `require_expression`'s only child in the path form is a `string_literal`, so the lane's whole read — `findChildByType(node, "bareword")` — found nothing and 912 dependencies over 5,913 files vanished with no trace. No count moved because `imports` was already non-zero from the `use Module` form. The construct IS a dependency and the path IS written, which is what makes it an edge rather than an inference. Caught by perl/ontology-require-and-universal, whose `require_file` row is the path form.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: an INTERPOLATED specifier is computed at runtime. `require "./lib/Late$stage.pm"` and `require "File/Spec/$module.pm"` name a different file on every run, so an edge to the written text is a fabrication. The rule is the ABSENCE OF A `$`, not the absence of a `./`, and it has to be stated because a path-shaped require is the shape that most invites the shortcut. Caught by perl/ontology-require-and-universal, whose first forbid row is the interpolated specifier.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: `UNIVERSAL::isa($obj, 'Class')` — the FUNCTION spelling of the type test. The grammar types it as an ordinary call, so the `method_call_expression` branch cannot see it, and `addCall` refuses it as a target because `isa` is a builtin. 157 corpus sites against 497 method-form sites, and the label it belonged to was already non-zero, so no count moved. Caught by perl/ontology-require-and-universal, whose first row is the function spelling and whose third row is the method spelling beside it.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: `can` is a PROBE, not a type test. `UNIVERSAL::can($obj, 'maybe')` names a method that may not exist, and `$obj->can(...)` is refused on the method side for the same reason; reading the function spelling as a `references` edge would carry a conditional probe into `bb_impact` as a real dependency. The two functions are one word apart and the argument is in the same position, so the refusal needs its own mutant. Caught by perl/ontology-require-and-universal, whose last forbid row is the probe.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: `push @EXPORT_OK, qw(a b)` — the Exporter's other declaration API, and the lane read only the assignment spelling. Measured: 11 `push @EXPORT*` sites in 8 corpus files, 6 of which carry literal names. A module's exported API was silently half of what it is, with no count to show it. Caught by perl/ontology-push-declarations, whose `pushed_one`/`pushed_two` rows are the word list and whose `pushed_three` row is the fat-comma spelling.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3, the DEFAULT this lane refuses: `push @EXPORT_OK, @Other::EXPORT_OK` pushes a NAME READ, not names, and publishing it as `exports` would put a variable in an exported API. 3 of the 11 corpus `push @EXPORT*` sites push something that is not a name — the other two are an indirect `@{ $EXPORT_TAGS{Parse} }` and a `@ISA` ref push — so a rule written from the SHAPE (`push`, then harvest words) fabricates three edges for every real one. Caught by perl/ontology-push-declarations, whose first forbid row is the pushed variable, and whose `uses` edge for the same read is the label that IS right.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: `push @ISA, 'Base'` — inheritance by push. The lane read `our @ISA = (...)` and nothing else, so 9 real sites carrying 10 base names over 5,913 files declared no inheritance at all (perl5's DB_File, Digest::SHA twice, Syslog, MakeMaker::version, Myconst2perl, Attribute::Handlers, CPAN::Shell, pkg_gen.t). It is worse than a missing `extends` edge: `packageBases` is what the OVERRIDE resolver reads, so those classes' methods had no base to resolve against either. Caught by perl/ontology-push-declarations, whose three `extends` rows are the three forms — two names in one push, the fat-comma spelling, and the qualified array.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: a QUALIFIED `@Foo::ISA` belongs to `Foo`, not to the package the file happens to be in. Attributing it to the enclosing package invents an inheritance edge for a class that never declared one, and the corpus has the shapes where the two differ — `push @UNIVERSAL::ISA, '...'` in perl5's Attribute::Handlers, `push @CPAN::Shell::ISA, 'CPAN::WAIT'` in CPAN, `push @version::ISA, "..."` in MakeMaker. Caught by perl/ontology-push-declarations, whose third `extends` row is inside a `package` BLOCK (so the lexical package is only inside the braces) and whose forbid row names the file-scope owner the edge must not land on.

PERL-ONTOLOGY part 3: `constant` is the name of CPAN's own module. The lane refused ANY dependency whose module name was `constant`, because `use constant NAME => v` is a DECLARATION rather than a dependency -- and that refusal was REDUNDANT for the `use` form, which the `use_statement` case handles as a declaration and breaks on before reaching it. So the guard only ever dropped real loads: perl5's `cpan/Scalar-List-Utils/t/dualvar.t:76` writes `require constant; import constant HAVE_THREADS => 1;`. The differential reported it as the single MISSING truth row in a 685-row file, and a guard whose stated reason does not apply to its own call site is the kind of rule that keeps costing. M14.6 regression: an `overrides` edge loses its line again — the pre-MR12 shape for all 8,085. M14.6 regression: an `implements` edge claims the line of the `with`/`use role` statement instead of the line the ROLE's name is written on. `use role 'R'` was stamped from the `role` KEYWORD's node, so a role named on a later line claimed the wrong one; and `with qw/
 MooseRoleOne
 MooseRoleTwo

Measured: 4 unexplained rows across a 14-file draw, all of them `with qw/`. Caught by perl/inheritance's role pins and by the oracle over the corpora.

PERL-MR4: a `use` argument list containing a top-level `=>` is a key/value SPECIFICATION, not a list of names to import. `use overload (q{""} => 'as_string', bool => sub () { 1 }, fallback => 1)` was recorded as items ["\"\"","as_string","bool","fallback"] -- a slot name, the handler the file must define, another slot, and a number. The `=>` is an anonymous token between the list's children and not a `fat_comma` node, which is why guarding `fat_comma` first changed nothing. Caught by perl/import-argument-items.

PERL-MR4: CODE IS NOT NAMES. A `?:` branch computes a value; it does not declare an import. In `use PluginList ('Plain::Plugin', '+Prefixed::Plugin', (eval { 1 } ? ('Conditional::Plugin' => { method_name => 'affe' }) : ()))` the branch contributed a plugin key plus two hash values alongside the two real plugins. Distinct from the fat-comma rule: that outer list has no top-level `=>`, so the argument COUNT was right and only the descent into the branch was wrong. Caught by perl/import-argument-items.
